passage:
Dear Bidisha,
I got the internship. The big consulting firm, the one Papa brags about to his office friends. I also made the dean's list. I should be over the moon.
Instead, I sat in the metro last night holding the offer email and felt nothing. Like I'd climbed a long staircase and found an empty room.
You asked me once, back in Class 11, why I needed to be first in everything. I said, 'Because then nobody can look down on us.' I think I've been chasing Papa's face lighting up, and the relatives' 'shabash', for years.
So I'm trying to write down what I would want if nobody ever found out. So far: teaching kids maths, building something slowly, having Sundays.
It's a short list. It's a start.
Love,
Sunaina

qa.q: What did Sunaina say in Class 11 about needing to be first?
qa.a: 'Because then nobody can look down on us.'

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel holding the offer email in the metro, and why?
qa.a: Sunaina felt nothing, hollow, because the success had been chased for Papa's pride and relatives' praise rather than for Sunaina's own wishes.

qa.q: What choice is Sunaina making now to redirect this ambition?
qa.a: Sunaina is writing down what would be wanted if nobody ever found out, starting with teaching kids maths, building something slowly and having Sundays.

qa.q: How might Bidisha respond to this letter, having asked that question years ago?
qa.a: Bidisha might feel touched that the old question stayed with Sunaina and want to support the new list rather than say 'I told you so'.

grounding: Shows a student who chased ranks and a big-name job for family approval, feels hollow after getting them, and begins asking whose approval was driving it.

passage:
You want the honest version, Vidya? In second year I ran for class rep, joined three clubs and bought a jacket I couldn't afford, all in one month. Not because I cared about any of it. Because the front-bench group noticed people like that.
And it worked. They waved at me in the corridor. My posts got likes. I won the election.
Then, the night of the results, I sat on the hostel roof and felt so flat. I kept scrolling, waiting to feel something.
My roommate asked, 'Tanuja, who were you trying to impress?' I listed names. Not one of them was someone I'd call on a bad day.
So I quit two clubs. I kept the rep job, because I actually like fixing timetables. I sold the jacket. Strangely, I sleep better now.

qa.q: What three things did Tanuja do in one month of second year?
qa.a: Tanuja ran for class rep, joined three clubs and bought a jacket Tanuja couldn't afford.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling on the hostel roof, and why?
qa.a: Tanuja felt flat and empty after winning, because the goals were about the front-bench group's notice, not Tanuja's own wishes.

qa.q: What turning point helped Tanuja change direction, and what did Tanuja keep?
qa.a: The roommate's question about who Tanuja was trying to impress; Tanuja quit two clubs and sold the jacket but kept the rep job, because fixing timetables is actually enjoyable.

qa.q: How might the roommate see Tanuja after these changes?
qa.a: The roommate may see Tanuja as calmer and more genuine, doing things for real reasons instead of for likes.

grounding: Shows a student chasing titles and peer approval who feels hollow after winning, then reflects on whose approval mattered and redirects effort.

passage: When the state engineering entrance results came out, Himani's rank was in the top hundred, and by evening the whole of Kotdwar knew. Her father handed out sweets; her uncle posted her photo in the family group; strangers stopped her outside the chemist's. She smiled for everyone. That night she sat on the roof with her friend Gargi and felt strangely empty, as if she'd climbed a staircase to an empty room. "I did it for Papa's face at the sweet shop," she said slowly. "I don't even know if I like engineering." Gargi didn't answer right away. Then: "What would you want, if nobody was watching?" Himani looked at the dark hills for a long time. She didn't have an answer yet.

qa.q: Where did Himani's uncle post her photo?
qa.a: In the family group.

qa.q: How did Himani feel on the roof that night?
qa.a: She felt strangely empty, as if she'd climbed a staircase to an empty room.

qa.q: What question could help Himani redirect her ambition?
qa.a: Gargi's question about what she would want if nobody was watching.

qa.q: How does Himani's father experience the result?
qa.a: He is proud and delighted, handing out sweets to everyone.

grounding: Shows a student who chased a rank to impress family and feels hollow after reaching it, prompted to ask whose approval she seeks.

passage: Beatriz had printed the logo of the city's most famous law firm and taped it above her desk in the São Paulo dorm. For two years she chased it: top grades, the right societies, the right parties. When the internship offer came, she posted a photo within minutes. Four hundred likes. Her mother called, crying with pride. Then Beatriz sat in her room and felt nothing much at all. Her roommate Mei, who was taking a lower-paid job at a legal-aid clinic because she loved the work, came in humming. Beatriz watched her, and a question she had avoided for two years arrived: whose dream is this? She took down the logo and looked at the pale rectangle it left on the wall.

qa.q: How many likes did Beatriz's photo get?
qa.a: Four hundred likes.

qa.q: How did Beatriz feel after getting the internship?
qa.a: She felt hollow, nothing much at all, despite the likes and her mother's pride.

qa.q: What step might help Beatriz redirect her ambition?
qa.a: Reflecting on whose dream she has been chasing and what work she would love, as Mei does.

qa.q: How does Mei seem to feel about her lower-paid job?
qa.a: Mei seems happy and content, humming because she loves the work.

grounding: Illustrates a student chasing a prestigious name for approval, feeling hollow on arrival and beginning to question whose dream it is.

passage: In the convocation hall of the engineering college in Coimbatore, Keerthana walked up for the gold medal while her parents filmed from the third row. She had planned this moment since first year: every late night, every skipped trip, for this. Afterwards, in the corridor, she felt oddly flat, the medal heavy against her chest. Uma-ma'am, her project guide, found her by the water cooler. "You don't look happy." "I thought I'd feel something," Keerthana admitted. "It was for Appa, I think. And for the girls who said I'd never make it." Uma-ma'am nodded. "And the chip-design work you did at two in the morning because you loved it? Who was that for?" Keerthana was quiet. Then, slowly, she smiled.

qa.q: Where did Keerthana's parents film from?
qa.a: The third row.

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel after receiving the medal?
qa.a: She felt oddly flat and hollow, the medal heavy against her chest.

qa.q: How did Uma-ma'am help Keerthana?
qa.a: By asking who the chip-design work was for, pointing her to what she truly loved.

qa.q: How might Keerthana's parents feel filming the ceremony?
qa.a: They are likely proud and happy, unaware of how flat she feels.

grounding: Shows a student who chased a medal for others' approval, feels hollow, and is guided to reflect on what she really values.

passage:
Dear Nandini Di,
You asked how it feels to finally be at the top college everyone at home talks about. I've been putting off replying, because the honest answer is: empty.
I chased it for four years. Rank 212. The name on my hoodie. Papa showing the admission letter to every uncle. For a week I felt amazing. Then it faded, and now I'm already worrying about getting the "right" internship with the "right" title.
Last night I asked myself something you once asked me: whose applause am I working for? Mostly Papa's. Some of it for the boys in my old coaching batch.
I don't know what I want instead yet. But I remember loving the electronics club in Class 9, building a radio that actually worked. Nobody clapped for that. I was just happy.
Maybe I'll start there.
Vishal

qa.q: What rank did Vishal get?
qa.a: Rank 212.

qa.q: How does Vishal feel now about reaching the top college?
qa.a: Vishal feels empty and hollow, after only a week of feeling amazing, and is already worrying about the next title.

qa.q: What question is helping Vishal redirect ambition?
qa.a: "Whose applause am I working for?", which shows it is mostly for Papa and old classmates, and points back to the electronics club Vishal loved.

qa.q: How might Nandini feel reading this email?
qa.a: Nandini may feel moved and glad that Vishal is being honest and using the question Nandini once asked.

grounding: Shows a student who chased ranks and titles for others' approval, feels hollow on reaching them, and reflects on whose approval drives the ambition.
